messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan is a 26-year-old detective who came to treatment months after leaving a violent marriage that, from the outside, had looked stable. He described repeated physical assaults by his wife that usually happened late at night after she had been drinking. What stays with him most sharply is not one single beating but the pattern: the sour smell of alcohol on her breath as she moved toward him, the moment he realized from her face that reason would not reach her, the blows, and the sounds that followed—her voice in a low, threatening tone, the slap of impact, his own breathing turning ragged. Because he works in law enforcement, he had felt especially humiliated by the abuse and deeply confused that he could read danger in strangers for a living but had not stopped it at home.

In the weeks after he moved out, the memories did not settle into the past. They remained vividly present, with an almost cinematic clarity that he found hard to explain. When they came, he did not just remember what happened; he sometimes heard it again in his head, especially her voice and the sound of being hit, as if the scene had broken back into the room. The memories forced themselves on him without warning. At work, if he interviewed an assault victim and noticed fresh bruising on a face or arms, an image of his wife standing over him would cut through his concentration. If a suspect or witness carried the smell of alcohol, the memory arrived even faster, complete and intrusive. At other times the trigger was in his own body: a wave of nausea would rise during a tense call or while driving home at night, and the nausea itself became a signal that the whole scene was about to flood back.

Those moments did more than bring back the assaults. They confirmed something Ethan had come to believe about the world. The sight of injuries on other people no longer registered simply as evidence in a case; it seemed to prove that people are not what they seem and that harm can be hidden inside ordinary intimacy. The smell of alcohol had become, in his mind, almost inseparable from betrayal. He said he had lost faith in people generally, not only in his former partner, and at times in life itself. Even around colleagues, he felt apart from everyone else, as though what had happened had marked him permanently and placed him outside the category of normal men.

That sense of being an outsider made the memories harder to contain. When he told himself that no one could really understand, the scenes returned with even greater force in private, vivid and unsolicited, as if his mind kept insisting on a reality he could not share. He was certain that people would either misread what had happened to him or quietly judge him for it, and this conviction left him alone with the sounds and images. The more he saw others as untrustworthy or fundamentally unreachable, the more the abuse seemed to remain immediate rather than over.

He responded by trying to shut down whatever might let those memories in. He stopped relaxing on purpose. If he noticed himself beginning to unwind at home, he would get up, pace, check locks, or turn back to work materials because letting his guard down felt dangerous. He also numbed himself emotionally; he spoke of moving through parts of the day flat and detached because feeling anything strongly seemed to open the door to hearing her voice again. Physical contact became especially difficult. When coworkers clapped him on the shoulder after a long shift or his wife’s replacement hand brushed his arm in casual affection—he is now separated, but not yet divorced, and still navigating contact from others—his body recoiled before he had time to think. Avoiding touch made sense to him because touch had become bound to the vividly recalled moments he could not control.

Over time these habits hardened his view of other people. Pulling away from touch, staying constantly braced, and numbing himself left him increasingly convinced that closeness was unsafe and that he did not belong with other people anymore. His marriage had ended, and he had become more isolated at work as well; other detectives noticed he lingered less in the bullpen and volunteered to handle tasks alone. The strategies that were supposed to protect him ended up reinforcing his belief that trust was a mistake.

They also narrowed his world in practical ways that kept him sensitized to the very cues he dreaded. Because he would not relax, his body stayed tense and easily unsettled, and nausea came on more readily during the day. Because he avoided ordinary contact, even small movements by others in crowded hallways or during field work felt abrupt and jolting, making him more alert to signs of injury, threat, and contamination. On one recent case he had to photograph a victim’s facial wounds while standing near an intoxicated witness, and he became so overwhelmed by nausea, the smell of alcohol, and the instant replay of the abuse in his mind that he had to step out and let a partner finish. That incident frightened him enough to seek help. He said he is afraid that if this continues he will lose his marriage completely, lose his footing as a detective, and remain permanently cut off from other people. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget, but to be able to be in his own life without every smell, wound, or bodily wave of nausea dragging him back there again.
